ap_psychology-m01.set_intro: A researcher surveyed 300 first-year college students about how they usually respond to stress and measured each student's perceived stress score from 10 to 50. Students were classified by the coping style they used most often. The table shows the number of students and the mean stress score in each group.

stimulus.description: Perceived stress score by main coping style

items.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the table?

options.text: Students who mainly used problem-focused coping reported the highest mean stress
options.why: Problem-focused students had the lowest mean, 24.

options.text: All three groups reported the same level of stress
options.why: The means 24, 31, and 36 differ.

options.text: Students who mainly used avoidant coping reported the highest mean stress, and problem-focused students reported the lowest
options.why: The means are 36 for avoidant, 31 for emotion-focused, and 24 for problem-focused.

options.text: Emotion-focused coping reduced stress more than problem-focused coping did
options.why: The emotion-focused mean, 31, is higher than the problem-focused mean, 24.

items.stem: Which statement identifies a limitation of using this study to conclude that avoidant coping causes higher stress?

options.text: The study used a survey, and surveys cannot be used to collect data on stress
options.why: Surveys are a standard method for measuring perceived stress.

options.text: The groups were randomly assigned, so the results cannot be generalized
options.why: Students were not randomly assigned to coping styles.

options.text: The sample of 300 students was too large for any conclusion to be drawn
options.why: A larger sample increases precision and is not a limitation of this kind.

options.text: The study did not assign students to coping styles, so differences in stress may reflect other factors or the reverse direction
options.why: A correlational comparison cannot show that coping style causes stress.

items.stem: A student who is worried about an exam makes a study schedule and asks the instructor for help with difficult topics. Which type of coping does this illustrate?

options.text: Emotion-focused coping
options.why: Emotion-focused coping manages feelings rather than the problem itself.

options.text: Tend-and-befriend
options.why: Tend-and-befriend is a response involving caring for others and seeking social connection.

options.text: Problem-focused coping
options.why: The student acts directly on the source of the stress.

options.text: Avoidant coping
options.why: Avoidant coping means staying away from the stressor.

ap_psychology-m02.set_intro: Researchers randomly assigned 70 adults with obsessive-compulsive disorder to twelve weeks of exposure and response prevention or twelve weeks of relaxation training. A clinician who did not know the group assignments rated each participant's symptoms before and after treatment on a scale from 0 to 40, where higher scores mean more severe symptoms. The table shows the mean ratings.

stimulus.description: Mean symptom rating (higher means more severe symptoms)

items.stem: By how many points did the mean rating of the exposure group decrease, compared with the decrease in the relaxation group?

options.text: The exposure group decreased by 10 points, which is 5 points more than the relaxation group
options.why: The exposure group's decrease is 28 − 13 = 15, not 10.

options.text: The exposure group decreased by 13 points, which is 9 points more than the relaxation group
options.why: 13 is the after-treatment mean, not the decrease.

options.text: The exposure group decreased by 15 points, which is 3 points more than the relaxation group
options.why: The relaxation group decreased by 5 points, so the difference is 10, not 3.

options.text: The exposure group decreased by 15 points, which is 10 points more than the 5-point decrease in the relaxation group

items.stem: Why did the researchers use a clinician who did not know the group assignments to rate the symptoms?

ap_psychology-m03.set_intro: In a trial, 90 adults with a seasonal pattern of depression were randomly assigned to use a bright-light lamp or a dim inactive lamp each morning for four weeks. Neither the participants nor the clinicians who rated mood knew which lamp was active. Depression ratings range from 0 to 60, and a larger decrease means more improvement. The table shows the results.

items.stem: If the improvement of the dim-lamp group reflects changes that occur without the active treatment, about how much of the bright-light group's mean decrease is attributable to the treatment beyond that improvement?

options.text: About 14 points
options.why: That ignores the improvement that also occurred in the dim-lamp group.

options.text: About 6 points
options.why: The bright-light decrease is 14 and the dim-lamp decrease is 8, and 14 − 8 = 6 points.

options.text: About 22 points
options.why: Adding the two decreases double counts improvement that is not due to the treatment.

options.text: About 8 points
options.why: That is the improvement in the dim-lamp group alone.

options.text: To increase the number of participants who report side effects

items.stem: Several participants in the bright-light group report headaches and ask whether they must continue. Which response best follows ethical principles?

options.text: Allow any participant to stop and arrange appropriate care if the headaches are troubling
options.why: Participants may withdraw at any time, and researchers must protect their welfare.

options.text: Move the participants to the dim lamp without telling them
options.why: Secretly changing the treatment is deceptive and violates informed consent.

options.text: Tell the participants that they must continue so that the data remain complete
options.why: Participants cannot be required to continue.

options.text: Assure the participants that headaches are never related to the lamp
options.why: Giving false information about risks violates informed consent.
